issue.title: Should AI stand in for one of the two experts who read a breast screen?
issue.question: Should the NHS let an AI take the place of one of the two human experts who read a woman's breast screen, and who should decide?
issue.summary: Recruitment has started at Cambridge, the first of 30 hospitals in EDITH, a trial of AI in NHS breast screening, according to BBC reporting carried by the Copenhagen Post. Today two human experts read each screen. Women in the trial are randomly put into one of three groups: two experts as now, or AI used in one of two ways, either to review after the expert or to rate the risk before the experts read. The trial's information says "All images will be looked at by at least one human expert", and a woman can decline AI and have two experts read her images without it. Government support is £11 million, and the trial is expected to run about three years.

news.headline: AI-assisted NHS breast screening trial begins taking in women, with up to 700,000 to be invited

poll.pollster: Focaldata (for King's Health Partners, Responsible AI UK and the Policy Institute at King's College London)
poll.finding: If an NHS-approved AI system disagreed with a doctor's diagnosis, 55% said a second doctor should review before any decision is made and 7% said they would follow the AI's advice because it may be more accurate. This is not the same question as whether AI should replace one of two screen readers.

bench.title: Keep two experts for some women; test AI with one expert
bench.answer: The Health Secretary signs a rule for the 30 EDITH hospitals. No trust may cut reading jobs or hours because of the trial; time saved goes to shorter waits. Volunteers are placed by lot: two experts as now, or AI with one expert. Letters say which. Scan data stays in the NHS; no private firm may profit from it. Provisional fail: the AI group finds one in ten fewer cancers, or more cancers showing up between screens, than the two-expert group. First check at 12 months, including waits. Stops 31 December 2029 unless Parliament renews it. Leaves out women under 50 or over 71, and any who decline AI. Two-expert women get no less than today.

bench.title: NHS-owned scan software, women told their group, staff can stop it
bench.answer: Inside EDITH's volunteer sites, the Health Secretary signs a rule: the NHS owns the software and every scan, and no firm may keep or sell them. Volunteers are picked by lot: two experts as now, or one expert plus the NHS-owned AI. Each woman is told her group. A woman can say no and keep two experts. No post is cut; time saved goes to shorter waits. Staff and women sit on a panel that can switch it off. Fail: if AI finds more than 1 in 100 fewer cancers than two experts, checked at 12 months, it stops. Ends 31 December 2029 unless Parliament renews it. Leaves out women who decline and women outside the 30 sites.

bench.title: Give local women the brake on AI screening
bench.answer: Your scan, your choice. Trial replacing one reader only with willing women, assigned by lot against two human readers. Each NHS unit needs approval from a local patient panel drawn by lot; its clinical director signs. Explain each woman's allocation. Keep staff, a named human contact and two readers for anyone declining. Contracts must forbid commercial reuse of scans. Publish results by ethnicity, age and deprivation, counting women missing from the trial. Provisional failure: fewer cancers found, more cancers between screens, or median waits not cut 10%. Review waits after six months; stop on 30 November 2029 unless Parliament renews after independent safety review. Patient panels can stop participation earlier. No national rollout on inconclusive evidence.

rows.test: Finds at least as many cancers as two readers
rows.note: no source needed: logic. Its stop line lets the AI group find up to one in ten fewer cancers, so it does not hold to "at least as many".

rows.test: Faster results, shorter waits
rows.note: Time saved goes to shorter waits and waits are checked at 12 months, but there is no fail number for waits and no evidence yet that AI shortens them.

rows.test: Women told plainly which screen
rows.note: no source needed: logic. Letters tell each woman which group she is in.

rows.test: Proper trial on real women first
rows.note: Volunteers are placed by lot between two experts and AI with one, as EDITH already randomises women into groups.

rows.test: Limit: no staff cuts, a human to ask
rows.note: Bans cuts to reading jobs and hours, and one human expert reads every image in EDITH, but no named person is offered for a woman to ask.

rows.test: Limit: no misses two readers would catch
rows.note: no source needed: logic. It accepts a drop of up to one in ten cancers found before stopping, so some women could be missed.

rows.test: Limit: no scans to firms for profit
rows.note: Promises scan data stays in the NHS, yet EDITH has a company-run cloud and AI providers handling images; the sources do not settle whether that can be met.

rows.test: Finds at least as many cancers as two readers
rows.note: Stops if AI finds more than 1 in 100 fewer cancers, so a small shortfall is allowed; whether AI matches two readers is what the trial exists to find out.

rows.test: Faster results, shorter waits
rows.note: Time saved goes to shorter waits, but no waits measure or fail number is set and no evidence yet shows AI shortens them.

rows.test: Women told plainly which screen
rows.note: no source needed: logic. Each woman is told her group and can say no.

rows.test: Proper trial on real women first
rows.note: Volunteers are picked by lot between two experts and one expert plus AI, as EDITH already randomises three groups.

rows.test: Limit: no staff cuts, a human to ask
rows.note: No post is cut and a staff and women panel can switch it off, but no named person is offered for a woman to ask about her result.

rows.test: Limit: no misses two readers would catch
rows.note: The 1 in 100 stop line is tight but still allows some misses; only the trial can show whether any happen.

rows.test: Limit: no scans to firms for profit
rows.note: Needs NHS-owned software, but EDITH uses a company-run cloud and AI providers; the sources do not show NHS-owned software exists or could be used.

rows.test: Finds at least as many cancers as two readers
rows.note: no source needed: logic. Its provisional failure is any fall in cancers found against two readers.

rows.test: Faster results, shorter waits
rows.note: no source needed: logic. Sets a measured waits goal (median cut 10%) with a review at six months; whether it will be hit is not yet known.

rows.test: Women told plainly which screen
rows.note: no source needed: logic. Each woman is told how she was allocated.

rows.test: Proper trial on real women first
rows.note: Willing women assigned by lot against two readers, as EDITH already does, with no national rollout on inconclusive evidence.

rows.test: Limit: no staff cuts, a human to ask
rows.note: Keeps staff, names a human contact and keeps two readers for anyone declining; EDITH already lets women decline AI and have two experts.

rows.test: Limit: no misses two readers would catch
rows.note: Stops on fewer cancers or more between screens, but a trial can only show a miss after it happens; no evidence yet either way.

rows.test: Limit: no scans to firms for profit
rows.note: Bans commercial reuse of scans by contract; EDITH says its cloud company holds data a maximum of 30 days and AI firms cannot take data out of the UK environment.

gate.verdict: No answer passes every test and limit: A fails two, and the rest turn on evidence that does not exist yet, since whether AI finds as many cancers is what EDITH is running to learn. What cannot be settled by facts is who bears the risk of a possible miss and who controls scans held by firms.

jury.question: If AI replaces one of two expert readers, who should carry the risk of a missed cancer, and who should hold the scans?
options: Trial it, with no cuts and no firm profiting
Local women get a veto before their hospital joins
Only NHS-owned AI, and strict stop numbers
Keep two human experts for every woman
jury.ruling: Trial it, with no cuts and no firm profiting (4 of 12). Jurors wanted the test run on real women before anyone takes the risk, and the no-cuts and no-profit rules mattered most to them.
